1:
When it was written neither Calvin nor Clarke will fix. Calvin doubts David was the author, since when he bewails the persecutions under Saul it is his habit to interpose some particular reference to himself; he takes it rather for a prayer composed for all the godly by some prophet, either in the Babylonian captivity or under the cruelty of Antiochus Epiphanes. Clarke reaches the same ground more briefly, calling it probably a complaint of the captives in Babylon about the contempt they received, the author being uncertain. What Calvin draws from that is the breadth of its use: the Spirit calls us to have recourse to God whenever wicked men proudly persecute, not one or two of the faithful only, but the whole body of the Church. Keil and Delitzsch tie it to the psalm before by the shared name Jahve our God, quote Alsted's title for it — the hoping eye — and call it an upward glance of waiting faith under tyranny, noting that its unusually rhyming form comes only from the inflexional rhymes which creep of themselves into the language of prayer.

The God addressed is described by where he dwells. Henry hears the lesson Christ taught in prayer, to have an eye to our Father in heaven — not that God is confined there, but that there especially he manifests his glory, as a king in his court; and heaven is a place of prospect and of power, since he who dwells there sees all the calamities of his people and can send to save them. When God seems to have forsaken the earth and enemies ask where now is your God, his people can still answer that their God is in the heavens; or, as some render it, sits there as Judge, to which throne injured innocence may appeal. Ellicott compresses the same thought into three words, O thou throned one. Calvin adds why the title is chosen: so that when no hope of aid is left on earth, and their condition is as desperate as if they were laid in the grave, they should remember that the power of God remains in heaven unimpaired.

Spurgeon makes the lifted eyes a confession of faith. It is good to have some one to look up to, and the psalmist looked so high he could look no higher — not to the hills, but to the God of the hills. He believed in a personal God, and knew nothing of that modern pantheism which is nothing more than atheism wearing a figleaf; the uplifted eyes represent the heart that fixes desire, hope and expectation upon the Lord. Gill takes the gesture inward as well as upward: not the eyes of the body only, this being a posture of prayer, but the eyes of the mind opened by the Spirit — the phrase expressing holy confidence, whereas men confounded by a sense of their sins cannot lift up their eyes to heaven at all.

Augustine hears one voice in it, and a homesick one. Let each of you be this man, he says, for since you are all one in Christ it is one man who speaks — not, unto thee have we lifted our eyes, but, unto thee have I lifted mine. What makes a Christian's heart heavy is that he is a pilgrim and longs for his country: though everything combine to make you prosperous and the world smile on every side you groan nevertheless, because you see yourself set in a pilgrimage and feel that you have happiness in the eyes of fools but not yet after the promise of Christ. This you seek with groans and longings, and by longing you ascend, and while ascending you sing the Song of Degrees. Where then are the ladders? We see so great an interval between heaven and earth, and wish to climb, and see none.
2:
What the servant's eye watches for they answer four ways, and Gill lists them all. It may be direction in the work, often given by a motion of the hand or a rap of the fingers without speaking; or help against enemies, since servants unarmed in their master's service have none else to flee to, which is Aben Ezra's sense; or food, which is how Kimchi and Arama take it, Arama observing that servants have their food in a way of mercy and not of justice; or simply their wages. Clarke adds two more. The words may be the language of readiness — we wait for thy commands, willing to obey them when made known; or of imitation, as servants watch to see how the work is done, that they may do it the same way, and so we watch, that we may learn of thee and do thy work in thy own Spirit. He notes a darker possibility, that the reference is to the chastisement of slaves, who while being punished keep their eyes fixed on the hand that inflicts it, professing sorrow and entreating mercy — a sense he thinks the following verse countenances.

Ellicott keeps the picture in the East. As the eyes of the slave are fixed on the hand of the master or mistress, waiting for a sign, so Israel waits for the least hint of divine interference to deliver from the tyrant; and he quotes Savary as exactly reproducing the poet's intention — the slaves stand silent at the bottom of the rooms, hands crossed over their breasts, and with their eyes fixed upon their master seek to anticipate every one of his wishes. Wesley reduces the waiting to two objects, supply of their wants and defence against their oppressors, and reads the until as lasting till he save. Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn at the next verse, where the second strophe takes up the plea for grace in echo, beginning with a cry for mercy confirmed in a crescendo after the form of steps; and they note that the intensive form used of a church abundantly satiated with ignominy accords with an earlier psalm of this group, probably by the same author.

On the plea itself the notes are brief. Gill observes that merit is not pleaded, for though servants they know themselves unprofitable ones; mercy is asked instead, and the repetition shows both a case requiring mercy in haste and the eagerness that makes the prayer fervent. Clarke hears a promise as well as a petition — chastise us no more, we will no more revolt against thee — and adds that the captives suffered not only grievously but contemptuously. Ellicott renders the measure of it as sated more than enough.

Who the scorners were each settles differently. Clarke names the Babylonians, who having subdued the neighbouring nations had none left to contend with them and grew luxurious, indolent and insolent. Gill describes them by their ease rather than their nation: men in affluent circumstances with more than heart can wish, without outward trouble or uneasiness about sin, at ease from their youth, their consciences seared and past feeling, though far from any true peace — and such men are generally scorners of the saints, loading them with gibes and jeers most insolently. Ellicott works on the text: the Hebrew makes a rare use of the article, best rendered by our demonstrative, this scorning, though the Septuagint's reading requires only one letter changed, removes an anomaly of construction and gives a better sense. He notes how the figure is kept to the end, the oppressors being the masters living in luxury while the slaves wait, quotes Gesenius citing Sallust on the wantonness of secure power, and says that reading the verse we seem to feel the whips and scorns of time, the oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely.
